text:
How to take Cornell Notes in Obsidian: Full Workflow

It is incredible to see that in the last month, 
@NickMilo
 video had over 50,000 views. This has generated much interest for Cornell Notes and raised some questions. Let me address some of them:

Isn't Cornell Notes an old paper-based system for note-making? Yes, it is, but the technique can just as easily be implemented in the digital realm. I like having a method built around Cues and Summaries that are independent of the note-taking medium. I use Cornell Notes in meetings when using a digital device isn't appropriate or when I want the flow of creativity that comes with paper and pen, but most of the time, I use this method in Obsidian.

Is Cornell Notes better than atomic notes, zettlekasten, and other XYZ methods? I think the question isn't which is better, but what is the proper method for the task at hand. Cornell Notes complement my other note-taking methods. I use multiple methods depending on the type of note, type of content, and the end result.  I prefer to use the right tool for the job. So it is good to have the basics. It is like a toolbox; I need a tool, but the one appropriate for the job.

Watch Nick's video to learn more about this technique to add to your toolbox of methods.

I also highly recommend trying the method on paper and doing it in your Obsidian vault. Having one method I can use in both the physical and digital realms is a joy.

Let me know if you have any questions about this method of note-making. #TfT
